description: I'm Artem, a full-stack developer and founder of TutPro, a learning platform used by 7,500+ students. I work with React, TypeScript, Python and 3D tools, and have won five international hackathons. We're building a lunar landing-site planner using NASA data to compare sunlight, terrain and communication windows. I'm looking for teammates interested in orbital mechanics, GIS, scientific computing, and UI/UX. I can lead development and pitching.
summary:
At the Moon’s south pole, choosing where to land is a challenge. A promising location may receive sunlight but lose direct contact with Earth behind surrounding terrain, threatening power availability and communication. Understanding these conditions across different locations and dates requires careful scientific analysis.

We developed LUNA (Lunar Landing Site Navigator), an interactive, NASA-data-driven application that makes lunar mission planning more accessible. Using NASA’s LOLA terrain data and JPL SPICE ephemerides, LUNA allows users to explore the lunar surface, compare candidate landing sites, and visualize how sunlight and Earth visibility change over time.

Beyond visualization, LUNA provides terrain-aware visibility analysis, estimates solar energy and communication opportunities, screens potential landing sites, and supports surface mission planning through an interactive 3D environment.

Designed for mission planners, researchers, educators, and space enthusiasts, LUNA transforms complex scientific data into an intuitive workspace for exploring mission possibilities. Our goal is to make early-stage lunar planning more accessible, transparent, and understandable.
details:
What We Built

LUNA is an interactive lunar exploration and mission-planning application developed for NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026.

At the Moon's south pole, even a promising landing site can face long shadows, limited solar energy, and interruptions in direct communication with Earth. These conditions depend on local terrain, celestial geometry, and mission timing.

LUNA brings these factors into a single workspace where users can explore the lunar surface, select candidate landing sites, change mission dates, and compare conditions across different locations.

How It Works

Users begin with an interactive lunar globe featuring NASA imagery and terrain information. They can select coordinates, configure mission parameters, and create two scenarios for side-by-side comparison.

LUNA uses NASA's Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter (LRO) Lunar Orbiter Laser Altimeter (LOLA) elevation data, alongside planetary ephemerides and NASA's SPICE system, to calculate the apparent positions of the Sun and Earth at selected locations and times.

The application evaluates how the local terrain horizon affects visibility and presents the results through interactive visualizations, timelines, and numerical analyses.

Its capabilities include:

  • Sunlight and communication analysis: Explore solar illumination, terrain obstruction, eclipses, and potential direct-to-Earth visibility windows.
  • Energy and communication modeling: Estimate solar-panel output, battery reserves, ground-station visibility, and radio-link margins using configurable engineering assumptions.
  • Landing-site comparison: Compare locations and mission dates, screen terrain slope and roughness, and explore candidate sites based on modeled environmental conditions.
  • Surface mission planning: Create mission schedules, plan rover traverses, avoid restricted terrain, and visualize illustrative surface operations.
  • Reproducible studies: Save projects, review NASA-based examples, and export results as PDF reports, structured data, maps, and mission schedules.
  • and lots more!

    P.S. you can find the full list of resources, datasets and science and/or maths formulas I've used at our website "Science" section.

Technology and Scientific Foundation

LUNA was developed using TypeScript, React, Vite, CesiumJS, and Python.

The interface uses CesiumJS for interactive lunar visualization, while a Python-based computational service uses NASA SPICE through SpiceyPy, NumPy, Rasterio, and PyProj for celestial geometry, terrain processing, and engineering calculations.

Scientific inputs include NASA LOLA elevation models, JPL planetary ephemerides, lunar orientation kernels, NASA Moon Trek imagery, and reference data from JPL Horizons. The project also incorporates historical NASA mission examples, including Apollo 17 and the Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter.

An optional AI assistant supports interaction with the workspace, while the scientific calculations remain based on explicit numerical models.

LUNA is open-source under the MIT License, allowing others to inspect the implementation and build upon the project.

What Makes LUNA Creative

LUNA connects multiple aspects of lunar mission planning within one interactive environment.

A user can explore a location, examine its sunlight and communication conditions, evaluate modeled energy requirements, adjust a mission schedule, and compare the results with another candidate site without switching between separate specialist tools.

The application combines scientific calculations with an approachable visual interface, interactive mission playback, customizable studies, and exportable results. This makes complex relationships between lunar terrain, mission timing, solar power, and communication easier to investigate.

Intended Impact and Considerations

LUNA is designed for mission-planning research, students, educators, and anyone interested in lunar exploration.

Its intended impact is to make early-stage landing-site assessments more accessible, support informed comparisons between candidate locations, and help students understand the scientific and engineering challenges of operating near the Moon's south pole.

During development, we considered scientific reproducibility, data provenance, terrain coverage, computational limitations, and the difference between preliminary assessments and validated mission decisions.

LUNA identifies missing terrain information and distinguishes modeled estimates from confirmed environmental conditions. Its results support research and education; they do not constitute flight-qualified predictions, guaranteed communication coverage, or landing safety certification.

More science about our project, including NASA datasets, equations, methodology, limitations, and source references, is available on our website: https://luna.tutpro.org/science.html

Project website: https://luna.tutpro.org/

PyProj = map projection and coordinate transformations
